correctness.rationale: For n>=4 there are exactly three degree-one pure and six degree-two nearly pure length-n multiplicity vectors, with every other vector of output degree at least three. Twelve codewords would force total incidence 24 exactly and hence all nine low-degree vectors plus three degree-three vectors; the nine saturate three of four parents at every monochromatic two-symbol observation, while each new degree-three vector contributes two such observations, an impossible six incidences in three remaining slots. Thus at most eleven. Three pure, six nearly pure, and the two distinct all-support vectors (n-2,1,1) and (1,n-2,1) have received-parent occupancies (4,4,3,4,4,4) in the declared order and attain eleven for all n>=4. At n=2, all six source multisets are admissible; at n=3, all ten are admissible because every received pair has precisely three parents. The actual reproducibility checker passed for n=4..128 and exhaustive size-twelve subset searches at n=4,5; independent integer optimizers verified selected further lengths. The symbolic all-length proof is independently sufficient and covers boundaries.

value.rationale: This exact, natural four-list deletion capacity is determined for every ternary source length n>=2, not a cherry-picked finite table or a routine restatement of the established unique-decodable bounds. It identifies the first sharp failure, when list size is raised from three to four, of the monochromatic-output upper bound for the two-survivor ternary simplex. The obstruction is a structural incidence lemma and the matching construction is explicit and uniform. This provides a useful and motivated exact benchmark for high-deletion list decoding; it does not claim a general theorem across arbitrary alphabet/list parameters.
